kurz: Tough connective tissue dissolves into gelatine in long, moist heat. That is why braising cuts turn meltingly tender after hours.
bild_im_kopf: Like a tightly knotted rope that slowly [[quellen|swells]] and loosens in warm water: force does not work, only time.
was_passiert: Connective tissue is made of collagen, very tough protein ropes. From about 70 °C they start to dissolve, but only slowly and best in a moist setting. They turn into gelatine, which can bind a lot of water and makes the meat seem juicy. The hotter, the faster, but too much heat squeezes out the muscle fibres.
warum_wichtig: Explains why shoulder, shin or cheek are tough when quickly fried and wonderfully [[zart|tender]] when braised.
faustregeln: Let the [[schmoren|braising]] liquid barely simmer, not boil.
In a pot at about 85–90 °C, count on 2–3 hours; in a slow cooker, 6–8.
It is done when a fork slides in without resistance, not when the clock says so.
typische_fehler: Taking braised meat out of the pot too early: it is then tougher than at the start.

praxis.text: Ragù, pot roast, boiled beef: cuts with lots of connective tissue need hours rather than minutes.
Simmered bones release gelatine into the stock. Cold it sets; warm it makes sauces silky.
